name: Battle of Tsushima
info: In the Tsushima Strait on 27–28 May 1905 the Japanese Combined Fleet under Tōgō Heihachirō destroyed or captured nearly all of the Russian Second Pacific Squadron under Rozhestvensky, and Russia sued for peace that year.

facts.place: The Tsushima Strait, east of Tsushima Island, between the Japanese island of Kyushu and the Korean Peninsula
facts.sides: The Japanese Combined Fleet under Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō, with over 40 vessels leading from the flagship Mikasa; the Russian Second Pacific Squadron under Admiral Zinovy Rozhestvensky, joined by the Third Pacific Squadron under Rear Admiral Nikolai Nebogatov, numbering 38 ships and outnumbered nearly three to one in total hulls
facts.outcome: All 11 Russian battleships were lost, seven sunk and four captured. Russian dead were more than 5,000, and the Japanese lost no heavy ships and had 117 dead.

t: The Russian fleet had sailed seven months and 18,000 nautical miles from the Baltic Sea, and it reached the strait with fouled hulls, crews with little training and a speed held to 9 knots by its slowest ships.
Japanese gunnery, high-explosive shells and wireless reports from scouting ships gave Tōgō the advantage, and four Russian battleships were sunk by sunset on 27 May.
Nearly the whole Russian fleet was sunk, captured or interned, and the Japanese lost three torpedo boats; the Treaty of Portsmouth followed in September 1905.
dyk: Oslyabya was the first modern armoured warship ever sunk by gunfire alone. One Japanese junior officer on the cruiser Nisshin, Takano Isoroku, lost two fingers in an accidental shell explosion and later became Admiral Yamamoto Isoroku.
ev: Japanese destroyers attack the Russian Far East Fleet at Port Arthur and the Russo-Japanese War begins
Rozhestvensky's squadron leaves Reval and Libau for the Far East, and the voyage takes it past the Dogger Bank, around Africa and on to Cam Ranh Bay
On 27 May the Japanese auxiliary cruiser Shinano Maru sights the Russian fleet and wireless reports reach Tōgō on the Mikasa
In the afternoon of 27 May Tōgō turns his line in sequence in the afternoon, Oslyabya, Knyaz Suvorov, Imperator Aleksandr III and Borodino are lost, and Rozhestvensky is knocked unconscious
From about 20:00 Japanese destroyers and torpedo boats attack the scattered Russian ships through the night
On 28 May Nebogatov surrenders his remaining battleships and Tōgō accepts after the signal flags are understood
The Treaty of Portsmouth ends the war
Britain begins construction of HMS Dreadnought

sections.background:
The Russo-Japanese War began on 8 February 1904, when Japanese destroyers attacked the Russian Far East Fleet at Port Arthur. Japan's first aim was to secure its supply lines to the Asian mainland for a ground war in Manchuria, which meant neutralising Russian naval power in the Far East. After the Battle of the Yellow Sea on 10 August, where Admiral Wilgelm Vitgeft was killed, and the Battle off Ulsan on 14 August 1904, what remained of Russian Pacific naval power was sunk in Port Arthur in December 1904.

The Russians then considered sending part of their Baltic Fleet east. The plan was to relieve Port Arthur by sea, join the First Pacific Squadron, overwhelm the Japanese Navy and delay the Japanese advance in Manchuria until reinforcements could arrive by the Trans-Siberian railway. The Tsar agreed to form the Second Pacific Squadron, five divisions of the Baltic Fleet including 11 of its 13 battleships. The Admiralty Council had opposed the dispatch, arguing that the Japanese crews all had combat experience and that training in the tropics would be practically impossible. At a council on 23 August 1904 Rozhestvensky, Navy Minister Avellan and the Tsar overruled it, since the coaling contract with a German shipping line was already signed.

Port Arthur fell on 2 January 1905, just after the squadron arrived at Nossi Be in Madagascar, so its objective became to join the ships at Vladivostok before bringing the Japanese fleet to battle.
sections.forces:
The Russian fleet had sailed over seven months and 18,000 nautical miles from the Baltic Sea. At the Dogger Bank it had fired on British fishing trawlers, killing several fishermen, and Britain almost entered the war in support of Japan. The fleet waited about two months each at Nosy Be in Madagascar and at Cam Ranh Bay, and its hulls were heavily fouled. The four new Borodino-class battleships had little time for crew training, and the rest of Nebogatov's squadron was older and poorly maintained. Russian ships had a top speed of 14 to 15 knots, and the auxiliaries 10 to 12, which limited the fleet to 9 knots. The Russians had a large advantage in battleships but were outnumbered nearly three to one in total hulls.

Tōgō's Combined Fleet put to sea with over 40 vessels. His 1st Battle Division could exceed 18 knots, and he had combat experience that Rozhestvensky lacked. His four modern battleships carried 16 Armstrong 12-inch guns with a range of 14 km and a rate of fire of one shot a minute, against 20 of the 1895 12-inch guns on five Russian battleships, with a range of 11 km and a rate of fire of 2.5 to 3 minutes in practice. The Japanese used high-explosive shells with Shimose powder, and a central fire control system introduced by Katō Hiroharu, while the Russians still used older armour-piercing rounds with guncotton charges.

The Russians had three possible routes to Vladivostok. Rozhestvensky revealed his choice of the Tsushima Strait only on 25 May, and the fleet approached in radio silence.
sections.course:
On 27 May, in fog, the Japanese auxiliary cruiser Shinano Maru saw the lights of the Russian hospital ship Orel and then the shapes of ten other ships. At 04:55 she wired the Combined Fleet command, and Tōgō received the message at 05:05. At 06:34 he wired Tokyo that the fleet would attack and destroy the enemy, adding that the weather was fine but the waves high. Scouting vessels sent wireless reports every few minutes. The fleets sighted each other at 13:40, and about 13:55 Tōgō hoisted the Z flag: the fate of the Empire depended on the result of the battle.

The Russians sailed from south-southwest to north-northeast and the Japanese from northeast to southwest. Tōgō ordered a 180-degree turn in sequence, and Rozhestvensky chose a formal pitched battle. At 14:08 the Mikasa was hit at about 7,000 metres, and she was hit 15 times in five minutes, but superior Japanese gunnery crippled most Russian battleships in thirty minutes. Oslyabya was the first sunk. By 14:45 Tōgō had crossed the Russian T. A hit on the magazines of Borodino by the battleship Fuji made her explode, and a shell fragment struck Rozhestvensky's skull. Nebogatov took command in the evening, the Russians having lost Knyaz Suvorov, Oslyabya, Imperator Aleksandr III and Borodino.

At about 20:00, 21 destroyers and 45 torpedo boats attacked for three hours. The battleship Navarin was torpedoed four times and sunk, and only three of 622 crew survived. Sissoi Veliky was scuttled the next day, and the armoured cruisers Admiral Nakhimov and Vladimir Monomakh were scuttled by their crews.
sections.aftermath:
At 05:23 on 28 May the Japanese sighted the remaining Russian ships heading northeast and surrounded Nebogatov's squadron, opening fire at 12,000 metres. The cruiser Izumrud fled. Nebogatov ordered his four battleships to surrender, knowing his guns were outranged and his ships slower. He hoisted XGE, the international signal of surrender, but the Japanese continued to fire because their code books lacked a signal for surrender, and a white tablecloth was then raised. Tōgō knew the signal meant a request for a truce, and his officers found the code book and reported that the engines had to stop. Nebogatov stopped all engines, and Tōgō ceased fire. Nebogatov told his men that the lives of the two thousand four hundred men in the ships were more important than his own.

Rozhestvensky, rescued from Knyaz Suvorov, had been moved to the destroyer Byedoviy, which raised a white flag when two Japanese destroyers caught it. He was taken to hospital in Sasebo. Until the evening of 28 May the Japanese pursued isolated Russian ships until almost all were destroyed or captured.

All 11 Russian battleships were lost, seven sunk and four captured. One tally gives 216 officers and 4,614 men killed and 278 officers and 5,629 men taken prisoner. Another gives 4,380 killed and 5,917 captured, with 1,862 interned. Three cruisers were interned by the United States at Manila. The Japanese lost three torpedo boats, with 117 killed and 583 wounded. Rozhestvensky and Nebogatov were sentenced to death at trials in Russia in 1905 and the sentences were commuted. Nebogatov was released in May 1909.
sections.sources:
The battle is known through the reports and recollections of men who took part on both sides, and through a minute-by-minute timetable kept in Japan Standard Time. Admiral Tōgō's own report describes how wireless let the Japanese follow the Russians' movements at a distance of 48 to 64 km through fog. Captain Vladimir Semenoff, a Russian staff officer aboard Knyaz Suvorov, described the shellfire that struck the flagship. Captain William Pakenham of the Royal Navy was present aboard the Japanese battleship Asahi as an official observer, and British intelligence also followed the Japanese fleet's training in the months before.

Estimates of Russian losses differ: one gives more than 5,000 dead and 6,000 captured, another 4,380 killed and 5,917 captured, and a third 216 officers and 4,614 men killed with 278 officers and 5,629 men captured. The causes of the Japanese victory are argued through a list of factors: experience, the salvo firing director, wireless, British support, high-explosive shells and gun range. Geoffrey Regan thought the result misleading, because the Japanese navy had performed well but its opponents were weak.
sections.legacy:
The battle was hailed in Japan as one of the greatest naval victories in its history, and Tōgō was revered as a national hero. His flagship Mikasa is preserved as a museum ship in Yokosuka Harbour. He was appointed to the Order of Merit by King Edward VII on 21 February 1906 and was made an earl by Emperor Meiji in 1907. The battle has been the focus of two Japanese films, from 1969 and 1983, and appears in the NHK series Saka no Ue no Kumo. It has been called the only decisive engagement ever fought between modern steel battleship fleets and the first in which wireless telegraphy played a critically important role.

It was the first defeat of a European power by an Asian nation in the modern era. Mahatma Gandhi, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, Sun Yat-sen and Jawaharlal Nehru were among the future national leaders who celebrated this defeat of a colonial power. Japan was established as the sixth greatest naval power and the Russian navy declined to one barely stronger than that of Austria-Hungary. Barbara Tuchman argued that Russia's loss destabilised the balance of power in Europe and contributed to the decision of the Central Powers to go to war in 1914. Geoffrey Regan argues that the victory created a legend that haunted Japan's leaders for forty years and set Japan on a path towards the Second World War.

Admiral Jackie Fisher reasoned that Tsushima confirmed the importance of large guns and speed, and in October 1905 the British began construction of HMS Dreadnought, which marked the beginning of a naval arms race between Britain and Germany.

summary: At Tsushima on 27–28 May 1905 the Japanese fleet under Tōgō sank or captured almost all of the Russian squadron that had sailed from the Baltic Sea, losing three torpedo boats. The defeat forced Russia to seek peace, and the Japanese navy's victory was widely celebrated.

notes: Contradictions in the article: the lead says one cruiser and two destroyers reached Vladivostok, the aftermath names the armed yacht Almaz (classed as a cruiser) and the destroyers Grozniy and Braviy. The lead says 'seven sunk and four captured' battleships; the battleship paragraph lists Navarin, Sissoi Veliky and Admiral Ushakov as lost to action or scuttled, and four surrendered.

Russian casualties are given three ways (lead: more than 5,000 dead and 6,000 captured; the 'Russian losses' paragraph: 216 officers and 4,614 men killed, 278 officers and 5,629 men captured, 79 and 1,783 interned; the next paragraph: 4,380 killed, 5,917 captured, 1,862 interned). I gave the three in the sources section and two in the aftermath.

First sighting of the Russian fleet is 02:45 (light of the Orel) in the prose and 04:45 in the timeline; the message time is 04:55 in the prose and 04:45 in the timeline. I used the prose and left out the 02:45 and 04:45 times.

The article says Oslyabya sank 'ninety minutes into the battle' but its timeline has her sinking at 15:10, about an hour after the first shots; I gave no time. Mikasa hit at 14:08 in the prose and 14:12 in the timeline; I used 14:08.
The lead's sentence about the Treaty of Portsmouth and '340 years after the first battle ... in 1565' is garbled; I used only the treaty and September 1905.

The article says Nebogatov's surrender was 'south of the island of Takeshima'; by instruction I left out the islet and the sea around it. I also left out the sea's Japanese name ('Naval Battle of the Sea of Japan').
Fölkersahm's death (24 May 1905) and the Dogger Bank inquiry details were left out for length. I gave the total as 'Japanese lost three torpedo boats, 117 killed, 583 wounded' as the article does.

The article gives no Japanese ship totals beyond 'over 40 vessels'; its Russian total '38' is for ships in the strait, while 48 left the Baltic. 'The article's 3:1' is the article's own phrase for total hulls. Nothing is claimed of Japanese strength in men.

'The only decisive engagement ever fought between modern steel battleship fleets' is the article's own lead claim, kept attributed as 'described as'. Please check that my wording in legacy does not state more than the lead.
